equivalents.note: Here nyi is the first half of the compound nyi zla, 'sun and moon', so the Tibetan has the sun share the moon's disc.
The Tibetan has one disc for sun and moon together (nyi zla'i dkyil 'khor, 'the disc of sun and moon'), where the Bengali names rabi and śaśimaṇḍala separately, each with its own na.
The Tibetan line has gzhan, 'other', for baṅka, 'crooked' ('do not take the other'), while its comment has lam kyog po, 'the crooked path' (cp.32.m3).
The Tibetan turns sāṅge, 'in the company of', into the verb 'grogs, 'keep company with', as its comment does for saṅgamena (cp.32.m5).
The Tibetan has no father: the vocative kye, 'O!', closing the line seems to stand for bapā, which the Bengali uses as a familiar form of address.

The comment has rang bzhin where the song line has ngo bo nyid, and makes the abandoning qualify it (rnam par rtog pa yongs su spangs pa'i rang bzhin gyis, 'by the nature that has wholly abandoned concepts'), where the Sanskrit has the mind freed by its own nature through abandoning them.
In Saraha's words the Tibetan renders avadhūtī by sense, kun spangs, 'abandoning all', where the comment on the refrain transcribes it (a wa d+hU tI'i lam, cp.32.m3).
The Tibetan renders caryāntara as glu dbyangs gzhan, 'another song', using the word its headings use for rāga.

The Tibetan reads akṣi vujhiā as 'seen by the eye' (mig gis mthong ba'i lam) rather than 'with eyes closed', as its line does with the same phrase in song 15, which these quoted lines appear to echo (khral sa for ghāṭa).

questions: citta (niamaṇa) at cp.32.3b: not matched. The Tibetan line has no word for 'mind': bdag gis bdag nyid nges par shes pas so, 'because one knows oneself by oneself with certainty', as if nia- were read as niyata, 'certain' (nges pa), with maṇa absorbed into shes pa, 'know'. Munidatta's nijamanasā is rendered rang gi yid kyi, 'of one's own mind', in the comment (cp.32.m4), where citta is already matched.
